subtitle: a pill that keeps fallout out of bone

effect: sponge-like crystals with a huge inner surface trap one chosen gas
how: After a reactor accident, iodine tablets protect the thyroid for a few days, but the other main fallout product, radioactive strontium, behaves chemically like calcium, settles into bone and irradiates the marrow for the rest of a life; nothing on any shelf stops it. The pill carries crystal sponges whose pores are built to the exact size and charge of a strontium ion, so they grip it harder than calcium and carry it out of the gut before the body can mistake it for bone material.
obstacle: Telling strontium from the calcium we need, inside a stomach's acid, is a chemically brutal distinction between two near-identical ions.
why: Fills the real gap in fallout medicine: everything after the iodine tablet.
real: MOFs with size- and charge-matched pores (crown-ether-walled MOF-18Cr6 at 99.7% removal, a 2025 Cu-MOF with ultra-high Sr selectivity against large excesses of Ca and Ba) exist only as wastewater separation studies, while oral strontium decorporation has been shown in animals only with alginate and Zn-InsP6; no MOF has been tested as a gut-binding pill.
